claims.claim: After stopping denosumab, spinal fracture rates rose to those of untreated women, and a larger share of those who fractured had several spinal fractures.
claims.supporting_passage: Cummings 2018 (Abstract): "Of 1001 participants who discontinued denosumab during FREEDOM or Extension, the vertebral fracture rate increased from 1.2 per 100 participant-years during the on-treatment period to 7.1, similar to participants who received and then discontinued placebo (n = 470; 8.5 per 100 participant-years). Among participants with ≥1 off-treatment vertebral fracture, the proportion with multiple (>1) was larger among those who discontinued denosumab (60.7%) than placebo (38.7%; p = 0.049), corresponding to a 3.4% and 2.2% risk of multiple vertebral fractures, respectively. The odds (95% confidence interval) of developing multiple vertebral fractures after stopping denosumab were 3.9 (2.1-7. 2) times higher in those with prior vertebral fractures ... The rates (per 100 participant-years) of nonvertebral fractures during the off-treatment period were similar (2.8, denosumab; 3.8, placebo)."
claims.location: Cummings 2018 Abstract, Results
claims.pico_timeframe: Postmenopausal women with osteoporosis in FREEDOM and its extension who had 2 or more doses of denosumab (n=1001) or placebo (n=470) and then stopped; followed 7 months or more after the last dose; post hoc analysis
claims.safe_wording: In a follow-up of a large trial, women on denosumab had about 1 spinal fracture per 100 women per year. After stopping, this rose to about 7 per 100 per year, close to the rate in women who had only ever had a dummy injection (about 8 per 100). Among women who had a spinal fracture after stopping, 6 in 10 had more than one, compared with 4 in 10 after stopping the dummy injection. Overall, about 3 in 100 women who stopped denosumab had several spinal fractures.
claims.qualifications: Post hoc analysis, not a randomised comparison of stopping versus continuing. Postmenopausal women with osteoporosis only. The 60.7% applies only to those who had a spinal fracture, not to everyone who stopped. Rates are per 100 participant-years. Non-spinal fracture rates were not higher after stopping. Do not say 'several spinal fractures at once'; say 'more than one spinal fracture'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Rebound risk appears greatest in people with a previous spinal fracture. The size of the rebound relative to never treated is modest (7.1 vs 8.5 per 100 participant-years); the distinctive feature is multiple fractures.

claims.claim: In UK primary care records, a denosumab dose delayed by more than 16 weeks was linked with a higher risk of spinal fracture than on-time dosing.
claims.supporting_passage: "Investigators identified 2594 patients initiating denosumab therapy. The risk for composite fracture over 6 months was 27.3 in 1000 for on-time dosing, 32.2 in 1000 for short delay, and 42.4 in 1000 for long delay. Compared with on-time injections, short delay had a hazard ratio (HR) for composite fracture of 1.03 (95% CI, 0.63 to 1.69) and long delay an HR of 1.44 (CI, 0.96 to 2.17) (for trend = 0.093). For vertebral fractures, short delay had an HR of 1.48 (CI, 0.58 to 3.79) and long delay an HR of 3.91 (CI, 1.62 to 9.45)." Conclusion: "Although delayed administration of subsequent denosumab doses by more than 16 weeks is associated with increased risk for vertebral fracture compared with on-time dosing, evidence is insufficient to conclude that fracture risk is increased at other anatomical sites with long delay."

claims.pico_timeframe: People aged 45 or over starting denosumab, UK THIN primary care database 2010 to 2019; next dose on time (within 4 weeks), 4 to 16 weeks late, or more than 16 weeks late; fractures over 6 months after the recommended date

claims.claim: Denosumab should not be stopped without a plan to switch to another bone treatment; the switch (for example a bisphosphonate) is started about 6 months after the last injection.
claims.supporting_passage: ECTS 2017 (Abstract): "Based on current data, denosumab should not be stopped without considering alternative treatment in order to prevent rapid BMD loss and a potential rebound in vertebral fracture risk." ECTS 2020/21 (Abstract): "In case of denosumab discontinuation, alternative antiresorptive treatment should be initiated 6 months after the final denosumab injection." NOGG 2022: "The increase in vertebral fracture risk following cessation of denosumab therapy emphasises the need to consider continued treatment with an alternative anti-resorptive drug following denosumab withdrawal. An intravenous infusion of 5 mg of zoledronate, 6 months after the last denosumab injection, reduces subsequent bone loss [...], although this effect is not seen in all patients and may not be maintained beyond one year, particularly in those who have had more than 3 years of denosumab treatment." Cummings 2018: "Therefore, patients who discontinue denosumab should rapidly transition to an alternative antiresorptive treatment."

claims.pico_timeframe: People stopping denosumab; guidance based on systematic reviews and expert consensus
claims.safe_wording: Denosumab should not simply stop. If it is going to stop, UK and European guidance is to plan a switch to another bone medicine, usually a bisphosphonate, given about 6 months after the last injection, when the next one would have been due.
claims.qualifications: How well the follow-on treatment prevents rebound is uncertain and seems to depend on how long denosumab was taken. The switch plan is a clinical decision; the post should not name a specific regimen for an individual.

claims.claim: In trials, bisphosphonates took about a year (12.4 months) to prevent one non-spinal fracture per 100 women treated, and about 20 months to prevent one hip fracture per 200 women.

The pooled meta-analysis found that 12.4 months (95% CI, 6.3-18.4 months) were needed to avoid 1 nonvertebral fracture per 100 postmenopausal women receiving bisphosphonate therapy at an ARR of 0.010. To prevent 1 hip fracture, 200 postmenopausal women with osteoporosis would need to receive bisphosphonate therapy for 20.3 months (95% CI, 11.0-29.7 months) at an ARR of 0.005." Conclusion: "These results suggest that bisphosphonate therapy is most likely to benefit postmenopausal women with osteoporosis who have a life expectancy greater than 12.4 months."

claims.pico_timeframe: Postmenopausal women with osteoporosis in 10 placebo-controlled RCTs of alendronate, risedronate or zoledronic acid; mean ages 63 to 74; time until 1 fewer non-vertebral fracture per 100 treated (or 1 fewer hip fracture per 200 treated)
claims.safe_wording: In trials of bisphosphonates, it took about a year of treatment before 1 in every 100 women treated was spared a fracture outside the spine, and about 20 months before 1 in every 200 was spared a hip fracture.
claims.qualifications: Trial women were aged on average 63 to 74 and were not frail or near the end of life. People with a very high fracture risk may benefit sooner, so the year is a guide, not a rule. Say 'in trials'.

claims.claim: People who usually continue beyond 5 years (oral) or 3 years (IV): aged 70 or over, previous hip or spinal fracture, high-dose steroid tablets, a new fragility fracture during treatment, or fracture risk still above the treatment threshold on reassessment.
claims.supporting_passage: NOGG 2022 summary recommendation 17: "Longer durations of treatment will be needed in those who are older (age ≥ 70 years), have had a hip or vertebral fracture, are on high-dose oral glucocorticoids (≥ 7.5 mg/day of prednisolone or equivalent over 3 months), or have a further fragility fracture during osteoporosis treatment." NOGG recommendation 6: "Fracture risk assessment in patients receiving drug treatment should be performed using FRAX with BMD ... If the FRAX-derived fracture probability exceeds the intervention threshold drug treatment should be continued". NOGG body text: "Post-hoc analyses from the alendronate and zoledronate extension studies suggest that women most likely to benefit from long-term bisphosphonate therapy are those with low hip BMD (T-score < − 2.0 in FLEX and ≤ − 2.5 in HORIZON), those with a prevalent vertebral fracture and those who sustained one or more incident fractures during the initial 3 or 5 years of treatment". Adler 2016 (Abstract): "In women at high risk, for example, older women, those with a low hip T-score or high fracture risk score, those with previous major osteoporotic fracture, or who fracture on therapy, continuation of treatment for up to 10 years (oral) or 6 years (intravenous), with periodic evaluation, should be considered."

claims.qualifications: The judge's point that NOGG lists a hip T-score of -2.5 or lower could not be confirmed from the extracted text: the NOGG flowcharts did not extract. The body text names low hip BMD (T-score below -2.0 in FLEX, -2.5 or lower in HORIZON) as predicting benefit from post hoc analyses. Use 'low hip bone density' or 'fracture risk still high' rather than quoting a flowchart threshold unless someone opens Figs 4 and 5.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Evidence for continuation criteria comes from post hoc analyses of two extension trials in mostly white women (Adler 2016).

claims.claim: In advanced CKD, especially on dialysis, bone fragility may be CKD mineral and bone disorder; high bone turnover raises hypocalcaemia risk; planning with the kidney team is advised.

Lloret 2024: "Management of osteoporosis for patients on dialysis should be centred in the dialysis unit because it needs to be integrated in the overall treatment of CKD-MBD []. Knowledge of bone turnover determines therapy choices in this patient population []. A high bone turnover calls for parathyroid hormone (PTH) suppressive therapy, particularly if the plan is to initiate (potent) antiresorptive therapy. High turnover bone disease is a robust risk factor for iatrogenic hypocalcemia ... Coordination of care in the dialysis unit should also include a post-denosumab hypocalcemia prevention regimen, which may involve (transient) increase of the calcium supply via diet, supplements or dialysate, ensuring adequate intake of vitamin D and close monitoring of serum calcium levels."

candidates.reason: All essential claims verified: 6-monthly dosing (NOGG full text); rapid offset after a missed dose (Cummings abstract, NOGG); FREEDOM post hoc absolute rates 1.2 to 7.1 per 100 participant-years after stopping (vs 8.5 after stopping placebo) and multiple fractures in 60.7% vs 38.7% of those who fractured (3.4% vs 2.2% absolute); do-not-stop-without-switch guidance with switch about 6 months after the last injection (ECTS 2017 and 2020, NOGG, Cummings). Lyu 2020 (UK, observational) supports the delay point for spinal fractures only. Per the judge, replace 'several spinal fractures at once' with the absolute rates, add the 'already overdue: contact the surgery now' step (marked as practical advice), and label the timeline 'Illustrative example'. MHRA 2020 was not opened and is not cited. This post owns the 'do not pause denosumab without a switch' point.

Essential claims verified: time to benefit 12.4 months per 100 women for non-vertebral fracture and 20.3 months per 200 for hip (Deardorff abstract); STOPPFrail v1 lists calcium and anti-resorptive drugs (including bisphosphonates and denosumab) as potentially inappropriate near end of life because benefit is unlikely within 1 year (Lavan 2017 full-text excerpts); alendronate routine (NOGG full text); denosumab rebound (Cummings, NOGG). Required edits: say the time to benefit came from trials in women aged on average 63 to 74, not frail people near the end of life; quote STOPPFrail v1 wording, not v2 (v2 criterion text not opened); remove the unverified calcium details ('chalky', 'twice a day', 'two large chewable tablets'); keep the denosumab caveat to one sentence (editor); add the judge's sentence that reviewing the drug does not reduce pain relief, falls care or comfort, marked as judgement. Greenspan 2015 may be used as the result that went the other way, with 'too small to settle the question'.

NOGG 2022 full text supplies the placeholders: plan 5 years oral / 3 years IV then reassess; continue (to 10 / 6 years) if age 70 or over, previous hip or vertebral fracture, oral glucocorticoids at 7.5 mg/day prednisolone or more over 3 months, a further fragility fracture on treatment, or FRAX still above the intervention threshold; lower-risk people may pause for 18 to 36 months; reassess after 18 months (risedronate, ibandronate), 2 years (alendronate), 3 years (zoledronate), or at once after a new fracture; routine holidays not supported. FLEX (clinical vertebral fractures only; non-vertebral 19% vs 18.9%) and HORIZON extension (morphometric vertebral only, 14 vs 30) verified from abstracts; Black 2020 supports falling AFF risk after stopping. The hip T-score criterion from the NOGG flowcharts could not be read (figures did not extract): use 'low hip bone density' or 'fracture risk still high' unless someone opens Figs 4 and 5. Denosumab in one clause referring to the C04-07 post, not as the ending (editor).

Rarity, warning pain, bilaterality, duration-related risk and the Black 2020 benefit-harm comparison (per 10,000 women over 3 years, modelled) are all verified, and the proportions (about 70% warning pain, 28% bilateral) come from Shane 2014 full-text passages, with the caveat that another series found warning pain in one-third. The central instruction 'X-ray both femurs' goes slightly beyond the UK guidance opened: NOGG says image the femur (full-length X-ray, isotope scan or MRI) and image the other femur if an atypical fracture is found. MHRA 2011 not opened; cite NOGG instead. Add that most thigh pain has other causes.
candidates.revised_angle: New thigh, groin or hip ache in someone on long-term bisphosphonate or denosumab: ask about it at every review, image the full length of the thigh bone, and if an atypical fracture is found, image the other side as well, because these fractures are often bilateral. If the X-ray does not explain continuing pain, MRI (or an isotope scan) can show an early stress fracture. Keep the rarity figures and the 149 hip fractures prevented versus 2 atypical fractures per 10,000 White women over 3 years (modelled), with the less favourable balance in Asian women.

candidates.reason: Verified: 41.1% vs 2.0% severe hypocalcaemia within 12 weeks in dialysis-dependent women aged 65 and over (Bird JAMA 2024 abstract, observational); risk of emergency-treated hypocalcaemia rises with CKD stage and with CKD-MBD (Bird Ann Intern Med abstract, which broadens the point to stage 4 to 5 without merging definitions); UK product-information monitoring as reported by NOGG 2022: calcium before each dose, and within 2 weeks of the first dose in people with creatinine clearance below 35 ml/min, with low calcium and vitamin D deficiency corrected first (this fills the placeholder); bisphosphonate renal restrictions (NOGG).
